title: Plant Pathology II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 400L Plant Pathology II curriculum, building on the general principles taught in Plant Pathology I (BOT308): principles and methods of plant disease management (cultural, chemical, biological, physical, host resistance, and integrated approaches), epidemiology, and named diseases of major Nigerian/tropical crops (cassava, cocoa, maize, rice, banana, tomato, yam, citrus) and their control.

questions.question: Plant disease management, as taught in Plant Pathology II, builds on the general principles of Plant Pathology I by focusing specifically on:
options: Practical strategies and methods used to prevent, reduce, or control specific plant diseases
The basic classification of pathogens into fungi, bacteria, and viruses
Koch's postulates and general disease cycle theory alone
Plant cell wall structure and function
questions.correct_answer: Practical strategies and methods used to prevent, reduce, or control specific plant diseases
questions.explanation: While Plant Pathology I covers causal agents and general principles, Plant Pathology II applies that foundation to disease management strategies and named diseases of economic crops.

questions.question: Cultural control of plant diseases refers to disease management achieved mainly through:
options: Modifying farming practices, such as crop rotation and field sanitation, to reduce pathogen survival and spread
Applying synthetic fungicides directly to infected plants
Breeding entirely new resistant crop varieties
Genetically engineering the pathogen itself
questions.correct_answer: Modifying farming practices, such as crop rotation and field sanitation, to reduce pathogen survival and spread
questions.explanation: Cultural control uses agronomic practices, such as crop rotation, sanitation, proper spacing, and timing of planting, to create conditions unfavourable for pathogen survival and disease development.

questions.question: Crop rotation is an effective cultural control method against many soil-borne pathogens mainly because it:
options: Deprives the pathogen of its specific host plant for a period, reducing inoculum build-up in the soil
Increases the pathogen's ability to survive in soil indefinitely
Directly kills the pathogen through chemical action
Has no effect on soil-borne pathogen populations
questions.correct_answer: Deprives the pathogen of its specific host plant for a period, reducing inoculum build-up in the soil
questions.explanation: By alternating unrelated, non-host crops with the susceptible crop, pathogen populations that depend on that host decline due to lack of a food source over successive seasons.

questions.question: Field sanitation, as a disease control practice, primarily involves:
options: Removing and destroying infected plant debris and volunteer plants that could harbour pathogens
Applying fertilizer to boost plant growth
Increasing plant density to outcompete weeds
Irrigating fields more frequently
questions.correct_answer: Removing and destroying infected plant debris and volunteer plants that could harbour pathogens
questions.explanation: Sanitation reduces primary inoculum sources by eliminating infected crop residues, diseased plant parts, and volunteer plants that can carry pathogens over to the next season.

questions.question: Chemical control of plant diseases using fungicides is broadly classified into protectant and systemic types; a systemic fungicide is one that:
options: Is absorbed and translocated within plant tissues, providing internal protection and sometimes curative action
Remains only on the plant surface and washes off easily with rain
Can only be applied to seeds, never to foliage
Kills insects rather than fungal pathogens
questions.correct_answer: Is absorbed and translocated within plant tissues, providing internal protection and sometimes curative action
questions.explanation: Systemic fungicides penetrate and move within the plant's vascular system, offering longer-lasting protection and, in some cases, curative activity against established infections, unlike surface-acting protectant fungicides.

questions.question: Bordeaux mixture, one of the earliest fungicides used in plant disease control, is composed mainly of:
options: Copper sulphate and hydrated lime
Sulphur and water only
Synthetic systemic triazole compounds
Sodium chloride and vinegar
questions.correct_answer: Copper sulphate and hydrated lime
questions.explanation: Bordeaux mixture, a classical protectant fungicide first used against downy mildew of grapes, is prepared from copper sulphate and hydrated lime.

questions.question: A major drawback of relying heavily and repeatedly on a single chemical fungicide for disease control is:
options: The development of fungicide-resistant pathogen strains over time
Complete elimination of the pathogen population forever
Immediate improvement in soil fertility
Elimination of the need for any other control method permanently
questions.correct_answer: The development of fungicide-resistant pathogen strains over time
questions.explanation: Repeated use of a single fungicide, especially with a single mode of action, exerts selection pressure that favours resistant pathogen genotypes, reducing the fungicide's future effectiveness.

questions.question: Biological control of plant diseases involves using:
options: Living organisms, such as antagonistic microbes, to suppress plant pathogen populations
Only synthetic chemical pesticides
Genetically modified crop varieties exclusively
Heat treatment of planting materials
questions.correct_answer: Living organisms, such as antagonistic microbes, to suppress plant pathogen populations
questions.explanation: Biological control harnesses natural antagonists, predators, or competitors of pathogens (e.g., beneficial fungi or bacteria) to reduce disease incidence in an environmentally friendly way.

questions.question: Trichoderma species are widely used in biological control of plant diseases mainly because they:
options: Act as antagonists that parasitize or outcompete soil-borne fungal pathogens
Are themselves highly virulent plant pathogens
Only affect insect pests, not fungi
Cannot be applied to soil or seeds
questions.correct_answer: Act as antagonists that parasitize or outcompete soil-borne fungal pathogens
questions.explanation: Trichoderma species are widely used biocontrol agents that suppress soil-borne pathogens such as Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, and Pythium through mycoparasitism, antibiosis, and competition.

questions.question: Host plant resistance, as a disease management strategy, involves:
options: Using or breeding crop varieties that are genetically less susceptible to a particular pathogen
Spraying resistant chemicals directly onto susceptible plants
Removing all plants from the field
Only applicable to viral diseases
questions.correct_answer: Using or breeding crop varieties that are genetically less susceptible to a particular pathogen
questions.explanation: Host resistance exploits genetic variation within a crop species to select or breed varieties that resist or tolerate infection, often the most economical and environmentally sound long-term control method.

questions.question: The 'gene-for-gene' hypothesis in plant pathology describes a relationship in which:
options: For every resistance gene in the host plant, there is a corresponding avirulence gene in the pathogen
Resistance genes only exist in pathogens, never in host plants
All plant diseases are caused by a single universal gene
Disease resistance is never inherited genetically
questions.correct_answer: For every resistance gene in the host plant, there is a corresponding avirulence gene in the pathogen
questions.explanation: Proposed by Flor, the gene-for-gene hypothesis explains specific host-pathogen recognition: resistance occurs when a host resistance (R) gene product recognizes the product of a matching pathogen avirulence (Avr) gene.

questions.question: Physical/thermal methods of disease control, such as hot-water treatment of planting materials, are commonly used to:
options: Eliminate pathogens carried within or on seeds, corms, or other propagating materials before planting
Permanently sterilize entire agricultural fields
Replace the need for resistant varieties entirely
Increase pathogen sporulation
questions.correct_answer: Eliminate pathogens carried within or on seeds, corms, or other propagating materials before planting
questions.explanation: Hot-water treatment and similar thermotherapy methods are used to disinfect propagating materials such as yam setts, banana suckers, or seeds of internally borne pathogens before planting.

questions.question: Soil solarization, a physical disease control method, works by:
options: Using clear plastic sheeting to trap solar heat and raise soil temperature to levels lethal to many soil-borne pathogens
Flooding the soil permanently with water
Applying synthetic fungicides beneath the soil surface
Freezing the soil artificially
questions.correct_answer: Using clear plastic sheeting to trap solar heat and raise soil temperature to levels lethal to many soil-borne pathogens
questions.explanation: Soil solarization covers moist soil with transparent plastic during hot periods, raising soil temperatures enough to kill many pathogens, weed seeds, and nematodes in the upper soil layers.

questions.question: Quarantine and legislative control of plant diseases mainly aim to:
options: Prevent the introduction and spread of pathogens into new areas through regulated movement of plant materials
Eliminate the need for any other disease control method
Directly cure already-infected plants
Increase crop yield through fertilization
questions.correct_answer: Prevent the introduction and spread of pathogens into new areas through regulated movement of plant materials
questions.explanation: Quarantine regulations restrict or inspect the movement of plants, seeds, and produce across borders or regions to prevent the introduction of exotic pathogens not already present.

questions.question: Integrated Disease Management (IDM) is best described as an approach that:
options: Combines multiple compatible control strategies (cultural, biological, chemical, host resistance) for sustainable, effective disease control
Relies exclusively on a single chemical fungicide
Uses only biological control agents and nothing else
Ignores economic considerations entirely
questions.correct_answer: Combines multiple compatible control strategies (cultural, biological, chemical, host resistance) for sustainable, effective disease control
questions.explanation: IDM integrates several complementary control tactics to achieve effective, economical, and environmentally sustainable disease suppression, reducing over-reliance on any single method.

questions.question: Plant disease epidemiology is the study of:
options: The development and spread of disease in plant populations over time and space
The internal anatomy of a single infected plant
The taxonomy of fungal pathogens
The chemical composition of fungicides
questions.correct_answer: The development and spread of disease in plant populations over time and space
questions.explanation: Epidemiology examines how diseases develop and spread through populations, considering host, pathogen, and environmental factors over time, underpinning disease forecasting and management timing.

questions.question: Disease forecasting systems, used to time fungicide applications efficiently, primarily rely on monitoring:
options: Environmental conditions such as temperature, humidity, and rainfall that favour pathogen development
The market price of the crop
The taxonomic classification of the host plant only
The colour of the crop's flowers
questions.correct_answer: Environmental conditions such as temperature, humidity, and rainfall that favour pathogen development
questions.explanation: Disease forecasting models use weather data, since temperature, humidity, and moisture strongly influence pathogen infection, sporulation, and spread, to predict outbreak risk and optimize control timing.

questions.question: Cassava mosaic disease, a major constraint to cassava production in Nigeria, is caused primarily by:
options: Geminiviruses transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
A soil-borne fungus infecting the roots
A bacterium spread through irrigation water
A nematode that attacks the tubers directly
questions.correct_answer: Geminiviruses transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
questions.explanation: Cassava mosaic disease is caused by whitefly-transmitted begomoviruses (family Geminiviridae) and also spreads through infected cuttings, causing characteristic leaf mosaic symptoms and significant yield loss.

questions.question: Black pod disease of cocoa, a devastating disease in West African cocoa production, is caused by species of:
options: Phytophthora
Fusarium
Puccinia
Xanthomonas
questions.correct_answer: Phytophthora
questions.explanation: Black pod disease, one of the most economically damaging cocoa diseases, is caused by Phytophthora species (notably P. palmivora and P. megakarya), which rot the pods and reduce yield.

questions.question: Cocoa swollen shoot virus disease (CSSVD), historically significant in Nigerian and West African cocoa farming, is transmitted mainly by:
options: Mealybugs
Whiteflies
Aphids
Soil nematodes
questions.correct_answer: Mealybugs
questions.explanation: Cocoa swollen shoot virus is transmitted by several species of mealybugs feeding on cocoa trees, and the disease has historically devastated cocoa plantations in West Africa, requiring tree removal as control.

questions.question: Maize streak disease, an important viral disease of maize in Africa, is transmitted by:
options: Leafhoppers (Cicadulina species)
Whiteflies
Aphids
Root-knot nematodes
questions.correct_answer: Leafhoppers (Cicadulina species)
questions.explanation: Maize streak virus (a geminivirus) is transmitted by Cicadulina leafhoppers, causing characteristic chlorotic streaking on leaves and significant yield loss in susceptible maize varieties.

questions.question: Rice blast disease, one of the most destructive rice diseases worldwide, is caused by the fungus:
options: Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia oryzae)
Phytophthora infestans
Fusarium oxysporum
Ralstonia solanacearum
questions.correct_answer: Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia oryzae)
questions.explanation: Rice blast, causing lesions on leaves, stems, and panicles, is caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (anamorph Pyricularia oryzae) and can cause severe yield losses under favourable humid conditions.

questions.question: Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) of banana and plantain, a severe vascular disease, is caused by:
options: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense
Phytophthora infestans
Puccinia graminis
Erwinia carotovora
questions.correct_answer: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense
questions.explanation: Panama disease is a vascular wilt caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense, which blocks the xylem and is notoriously difficult to control once established in soil.

questions.question: Late blight of potato, historically responsible for the Irish potato famine of the 1840s, is caused by:
options: Phytophthora infestans
Fusarium oxysporum
Xanthomonas campestris
Puccinia striiformis
questions.correct_answer: Phytophthora infestans
questions.explanation: Late blight, caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, destroyed potato crops during the 1840s Irish famine and remains a serious disease of potato and tomato today.

questions.question: Bacterial wilt of tomato and other solanaceous crops, a serious soil-borne disease in tropical regions, is caused by:
options: Ralstonia solanacearum
Magnaporthe oryzae
Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense
Cicadulina mbila
questions.correct_answer: Ralstonia solanacearum
questions.explanation: Bacterial wilt, caused by the soil-borne bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum, blocks the vascular system and causes rapid wilting of tomato, pepper, and other solanaceous crops, especially in warm, wet conditions.

questions.question: Yam anthracnose disease, an important foliar disease affecting yam (Dioscorea species) production, is caused by:
options: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides
Ralstonia solanacearum
Magnaporthe oryzae
Puccinia graminis
questions.correct_answer: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides
questions.explanation: Yam anthracnose, causing leaf spots, vine dieback, and reduced tuber yield, is caused by the fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporioides and is a major constraint on yam production in West Africa.

questions.question: Cercospora leaf spot is a common fungal disease affecting cowpea and several other crops, characterized mainly by:
options: Necrotic, often circular leaf spots that reduce photosynthetic leaf area
Wilting of the entire plant within hours
Swelling of the root system only
Discoloration of the flower petals exclusively
questions.correct_answer: Necrotic, often circular leaf spots that reduce photosynthetic leaf area
questions.explanation: Cercospora species cause characteristic leaf spot lesions that reduce the plant's photosynthetic surface area, weakening the plant and reducing yield if severe.

questions.question: Citrus canker, a bacterial disease affecting citrus crops, is caused by:
options: Xanthomonas citri (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri)
Ralstonia solanacearum
Fusarium oxysporum
Colletotrichum gloeosporioides
questions.correct_answer: Xanthomonas citri (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri)
questions.explanation: Citrus canker is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas citri, producing raised, corky lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit, and is subject to strict quarantine regulations in many countries.

questions.question: Downy mildew of maize, an important disease in humid tropical maize-growing regions, is caused mainly by species of:
options: Peronosclerospora
Puccinia
Xanthomonas
Fusarium
questions.correct_answer: Peronosclerospora
questions.explanation: Downy mildew diseases of maize in the tropics are caused by oomycete pathogens in the genus Peronosclerospora, producing characteristic chlorotic striping and stunting of infected plants.

questions.question: Post-harvest diseases, which cause rotting of stored fruits, tubers, and grains, are of major economic concern mainly because they:
options: Occur after the crop has already been harvested, directly reducing marketable yield and food availability
Only affect plants that are still growing in the field
Can be entirely prevented by crop rotation alone
Never involve fungal pathogens
questions.correct_answer: Occur after the crop has already been harvested, directly reducing marketable yield and food availability
questions.explanation: Post-harvest diseases (e.g., storage rots caused by Aspergillus, Rhizopus, and other fungi) destroy already-harvested produce, directly reducing food security and farmer income since the crop investment has already been made.

questions.question: Proper curing and drying of harvested grains and tubers before storage is an important disease control measure mainly because it:
options: Reduces moisture content, creating conditions less favourable for fungal growth and mycotoxin production
Increases the pathogen's ability to infect the produce
Has no effect on post-harvest fungal development
Is only necessary for fresh vegetables, not grains or tubers
questions.correct_answer: Reduces moisture content, creating conditions less favourable for fungal growth and mycotoxin production
questions.explanation: Lowering moisture content through proper drying inhibits the growth of storage fungi such as Aspergillus flavus, reducing rot and the risk of mycotoxin (e.g., aflatoxin) contamination during storage.

questions.question: Striga species (witchweed), parasitic weeds affecting cereal crops such as maize and sorghum in Nigeria, cause damage to their host primarily by:
options: Attaching to host roots via haustoria and withdrawing water, nutrients, and photosynthates from the host plant
Directly infecting the host through airborne fungal spores
Producing toxins that only affect the host's leaves
Being transmitted exclusively through insect vectors
questions.correct_answer: Attaching to host roots via haustoria and withdrawing water, nutrients, and photosynthates from the host plant
questions.explanation: Striga is a hemiparasitic flowering plant that forms haustorial connections with host cereal roots, diverting water, nutrients, and assimilates, severely stunting and often killing the host crop.
